title: Fix RandomForestClassifier ties in binary classification
description:
Fixes #58.

What was happening was that we were breaking ties (exact 0.5/0.5 probabilities) in accordance to what ONNX wanted it, but ONNX and scikit-learn disagreed on how to do that.

ONNX breaks ties up to class 1, and scikit-learn breaks ties down to class 0.

ONNX stores leaf weights as float32 (1/n_estimators becomes 0.10000000149…), so a vote split that should sum to exactly 0.5 comes out as 0.50000000745 once promoted to double, spilling genuine ties over the threshold.

title: Update duckdb requirement from ~=1.4.1 to >=1.4.1,<1.6.0
description:
Updates the requirements on [duckdb](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb-python) to permit the latest version.
Release notes

Sourced from duckdb's releases.

DuckDB Python 1.5.0 "Variegata"

This is the 1.5.0 release of DuckDB's Python bindings. For a list of changes in DuckDB core, have a look at the DuckDB release notes and the blogpost.

Breaking Changes

  • Dropped Python 3.9 support. The minimum supported version is now Python 3.10.
  • Removed deprecated duckdb.typing and duckdb.functional modules. These were deprecated in 1.4.0. Use duckdb.sqltypes and duckdb.func instead.
  • Renamed column parameter to expression in relational API functions (e.g., min, max, sum, mean, etc.) to better reflect that these accept expressions, not just column names.
  • Deprecated fetch_arrow_table() and fetch_record_batch() on connections and relations. Use the new to_arrow_table() and to_arrow_reader() methods instead.

New Features

  • Polars LazyFrame projection and filter pushdown. DuckDB can now push down projections and filters when scanning Polars LazyFrames, including support for cast nodes and unstrict casts.
  • Polars Int128 / UInt128 support.
  • VARIANT type support — Python conversion, NumPy array wrapping, and type stubs.
  • TIME_NS type support — nanosecond-precision time values across Python, NumPy, and Spark type systems.
  • Profiling API — new get_profiling_info() and get_profiling_json() methods on connections, plus a refactored query_graph module with improved HTML visualization (dark mode, expandable phases, depth).
  • to_arrow_table() and to_arrow_reader() — new methods on connections and relations as the preferred Arrow export API.

Performance

  • __arrow_c_stream__ on relations — relations now export via the Arrow PyCapsule interface using PhysicalArrowCollector for zero-copy streaming.
  • Unified Arrow stream scanning via __arrow_c_stream__, with filter pushdown only when pyarrow is present.
  • Arrow schema caching to avoid repeated lookups during scanning.
  • Arrow object type caching to avoid repeated detection.
  • Empty params treated as None for .sql() — avoids unnecessary parameter binding overhead.
  • Simplified GIL management for FetchRow.

Bug Fixes

  • Fixed Python object leak in scalar UDFs — PyObject_CallObject return values are now properly stolen to avoid reference count leaks.
  • Fixed reference cycle between connections and relations that could prevent garbage collection.
  • Relations now hold a reference to their connection, preventing premature connection closure.
  • Fixed fsspec race condition in the Python filesystem implementation.
  • Fixed numeric conversion logic — improved handling of large integers (fallback to VARCHAR) and UNION types.
  • pyarrow.dataset import is now optional — no longer fails if pyarrow is installed without the dataset module.
  • Thrown a reasonable error when an Arrow array stream has already been consumed.

Build & Packaging

  • jemalloc enabled on Linux x86_64 only (aligned with DuckDB core), removed as a separately bundled extension.
  • MSVC runtime linked statically on Windows — eliminates the VS2019 workaround from duckdb/duckdb#17991.

title: Skip constant tree columns in the separate_trees layout
description:
## What this does

`export_sql(..., separate_trees=True)` materialises each tree's contribution as its own column so columnar engines can evaluate them in parallel. Some of those contributions are constants: the ibis optimizer has already folded them to a literal before the layout runs. A column holding a literal computes nothing, so it spends SQL size and a parallel slot on a value the engine could inline. This skips them and leaves the literal inline.

Two cases produce them, and both are ordinary rather than exotic:

- Ensembles that fit one tree per class per boosting iteration. Each tree votes for a single class, so its votes for every other class are structurally zero. A 3-class `GradientBoostingClassifier` with `n_estimators=4` fits 12 trees, each carrying 3 votes: 36 candidate columns, of which 12 compute anything.
- Stumps holding a single leaf, where the whole tree is one constant.

## How

A new `folded_to_constant()` in `translation/steps/trees/tree.py` reports whether an expression reduced to a literal. `classifier.py` and `regressor.py` build the list of positions worth preserving, call `preserve()` once for those, and write the results back in place.

Predictions are unchanged. Only which values get their own SQL column changes, and a folded literal is inlined at the same value it would have had in a column.

## What it saves today

Measured on `main` versus this branch, iris, `separate_trees=True`, duckdb dialect:

| pipeline | tree columns | SQL chars | export time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3-class `GradientBoostingClassifier`, n=50 | 450 → **150** | 73,724 → **62,024** | 0.58s → **0.40s** |
| binary `GradientBoostingClassifier`, n=50 | 50 → 50 | unchanged | unchanged |
| `GradientBoostingRegressor`, n=50 | 50 → 50 | unchanged | unchanged |
| 3-class `RandomForestClassifier`, n=20 | 60 → 60 | unchanged | unchanged |
| 3-class `DecisionTreeClassifier` | 3 → 3 | unchanged | unchanged |
| stump-only regressor, n=20 | 0 → 0 | 70 → 60 | unchanged |

Column and character counts are deterministic. The export times are single runs and wander by a few hundredths between repeats, so treat them as a direction rather than a benchmark.

<details>
<summary>Script that produces the table</summary>

Run it once on `main` and once on this branch.

```python
"""Measure the separate_trees layout: per-tree columns, SQL size, export time."""

import time

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    GradientBoostingClassifier,
    GradientBoostingRegressor,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

import orbital
import orbital.types

iris = load_iris()
NAMES = ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"]
X = pd.DataFrame(iris.data, columns=NAMES)
FEATURES = {name: orbital.types.FloatColumnType() for name in NAMES}


def report(label, estimator, y):
    pipeline = Pipeline([("m", estimator)])
    pipeline.fit(X, y)
    parsed = orbital.parse_pipeline(pipeline, features=FEATURES)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    sql = orbital.export_sql("data", parsed, dialect="duckdb", separate_trees=True)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

    print(
        f"{label:<44} tree_cols={sql.count('AS \"tre_'):>4}"
        f"  chars={len(sql):>6}  export={elapsed:.2f}s"
    )


report(
    "3-class GradientBoostingClassifier, n=50",
    GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=50, random_state=0),
    iris.target,
)
report(
    "binary GradientBoostingClassifier, n=50",
    GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=50, random_state=0),
    (iris.target == 1).astype(int),
)
report(

```

Output on `main`:

```
3-class GradientBoostingClassifier, n=50     tree_cols= 450  chars= 73724  export=0.53s
binary GradientBoostingClassifier, n=50      tree_cols=  50  chars= 20348  export=0.14s
GradientBoostingRegressor, n=50              tree_cols=  50  chars= 27388  export=0.12s
3-class RandomForestClassifier, n=20         tree_cols=  60  chars= 26076  export=0.17s
3-class DecisionTreeClassifier               tree_cols=   3  chars=  2314  export=0.02s

```

Output on this branch:

```
3-class GradientBoostingClassifier, n=50     tree_cols= 150  chars= 62024  export=0.38s
binary GradientBoostingClassifier, n=50      tree_cols=  50  chars= 20348  export=0.11s
GradientBoostingRegressor, n=50              tree_cols=  50  chars= 27388  export=0.15s
3-class RandomForestClassifier, n=20         tree_cols=  60  chars= 26076  export=0.14s
3-class DecisionTreeClassifier               tree_cols=   3  chars=  2314  export=0.02s
stump-only GradientBoostingRegressor, n=20   tree_cols=   0  chars=    60  export=0.00s
```

</details>

### Where the 450 columns came from

`GradientBoostingClassifier` fits one tree per class per boosting iteration, so 50 estimators over 3 classes is 150 trees. skl2onnx puts all 150 into a single `TreeEnsembleClassifier`, and orbital's translator builds a vote per class for every tree, which is 450 expressions.

But each tree only ever votes for the one class it was fitted for. `build_tree_case` reads leaf weights with `node["weight"].get(clslabel, 0.0)`, so for the two classes a tree does not serve, every leaf yields a literal `0.0`. Both arms of every `CASE` are then the same literal, `optimizer.fold_case` collapses the whole nested `CASE` to `Literal(0.0)`, and what is left is a constant that no longer references the input columns at all.

Before this change the layout named all 450 of those as columns, so 300 of them came out as `0.0E0 AS "tre_NNN"`: an alias, a projection slot, and a name to resolve, wrapping a zero. Worse, each was then referenced again downstream, because the per-class sum added the column instead of the literal.

That second part is the real cost. Naming a folded literal as a column converts it from something the optimizer can fold into a column reference it cannot, so the zero survives twice over. Skipping the column lets the zero stay a literal in the sum, where `x + 0.0` collapses. Checked on an 8-estimator 3-class model: `main` emits 24 `CASE` columns plus 48 literal ones and contains 48 occurrences of `0.0E0`, while this branch emits the 24 `CASE` columns and contains no `0.0E0` at all. The zeros do not move inline, they disappear.

The same 1-in-3 ratio holds at any size, and it gets worse with more classes: at 5 classes, 4 of every 5 votes are constant.

### The smallest case that shows it

One estimator, three classes, default depth, `separate_trees=True`. That is 3 trees and 9 votes. Here is the per-tree CTE on `main`. The two long `CASE` bodies are elided and the leaf values shortened (they print in full float32 precision, `0.20000000298023224E0` and so on), but the column list is verbatim:

```sql
"t2" AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN "t1"."cnc_v5" THEN 0.2 ELSE -0.1 END AS "tre_v12",
    0.0E0 AS "tre_v13",
    0.0E0 AS "tre_v14",
    0.0E0 AS "tre_v15",
    CASE WHEN "t1"."cnc_v5" THEN -0.1 ELSE CASE ... END END AS "tre_v16",
    0.0E0 AS "tre_v17",
    0.0E0 AS "tre_v18",
    0.0E0 AS "tre_v19",
    CASE WHEN "t1"."cnc_v6" THEN CASE ... END ELSE CASE ... END END AS "tre_v20"
  FROM "t1" AS "t1"
)
```

Six of the nine columns are the literal `0.0E0`. Tree 1 votes for class 0 and hands classes 1 and 2 a zero, and so on down the diagonal. The same CTE on this branch:

```sql
"t2" AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN "t1"."cnc_v5" THEN 0.2 ELSE -0.1 END AS "tre_v12",
    CASE WHEN "t1"."cnc_v5" THEN -0.1 ELSE CASE ... END END AS "tre_v13",
    CASE WHEN "t1"."cnc_v6" THEN CASE ... END ELSE CASE ... END END AS "tre_v14"
  FROM "t1" AS "t1"
)
```

Three columns, one per tree, which is what `separate_trees` is asking for. Total SQL for the whole query: 3,333 characters before, 2,989 after.

To reproduce:

```python
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
import pandas as pd, orbital, orbital.types

iris = load_iris()
names = ["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"]
X = pd.DataFrame(iris.data, columns=names)

pipeline = Pipeline([("gbm", GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=1, random_state=0))])
pipeline.fit(X, iris.target)

parsed = orbital.parse_pipeline(
    pipeline, features={n: orbital.types.FloatColumnType() for n in names}
)
sql = orbital.export_sql("data", parsed, dialect="duckdb", separate_trees=True)
print(sql)
```

To print just the per-tree CTE shown above, rather than the whole query:

```python
import sqlglot

for cte in sqlglot.parse_one(sql, read="duckdb").find_all(sqlglot.exp.CTE):
    if "tre_" in cte.sql():
        print(cte.sql(dialect="duckdb", pretty=True))
        break
print("total SQL chars:", len(sql))
```

### Why the character count drops much less than the column count

Columns fall by 67% but SQL size only by 16%, which is the expected shape rather than a discrepancy. What goes away is short: a projection item of the form `0.0E0 AS "tre_NNN"` plus the reference to it in the sum, around 39 characters per vote across both. The bulk of the SQL is the 150 real trees' nested `CASE` expressions, and those are untouched. The export-time gain comes from ibis and sqlglot having 300 fewer projection items to build and compile, not from smaller trees.

### Why nothing else moves

One case does get marginally bigger, and it is worth knowing about. With very shallow trees (`max_depth=1`) the whole per-tree projection collapses on `main`: no `tre_` columns are emitted at all, the votes are inlined into the per-class sums, and the constants show up there as a `+ 0.0` term. This branch keeps the projection, so a 2-estimator 3-class depth-1 model goes from 2,518 to 2,707 characters (reproduce by passing `n_estimators=2, max_depth=1` to the classifier in the snippet above). That is the layout doing what was asked of it, materialising 6 per-tree columns where `main` silently materialised none, rather than a regression.

Otherwise: random forest trees vote for every class, so no vote folds. Binary classification takes the ONNX single-weight path, where `classlabels` is trimmed to one entry and there is one vote per tree. Regression has one value per tree. In all three cases there is nothing constant to skip. The stump case is already nearly free on `main`, since those trees emit no per-tree columns either way; the test for it is a boundary condition rather than a saving.

Note that `separate_trees` defaults to `False` in both `export_sql` and `translate`, so this only reaches callers who opt in.

## Relationship to the XGBoost work

This was found while adding XGBoost support

title: Make scikit-learn an optional dependency
description:
Closes #113

## Background

orbital translates scikit-learn pipelines and PyTorch models into SQL. PyTorch support is already an extra (`orbital[pytorch]`), but scikit-learn, skl2onnx and packaging were unconditional core dependencies. A user who only needs `parse_pytorch_model` still pulled in scikit-learn and skl2onnx.

## What changes

**Packaging**
- Core dependencies are now `packaging`, `onnx`, `ibis-framework`. `packaging` stays because `ibis.backends.sql.compilers.datafusion` imports `packaging.version` while ibis declares it only in backend extras (the previous comment attributed it to skl2onnx, which does not import it).
- New extra `sklearn = ["scikit-learn", "skl2onnx~=1.20.0"]`; `dev` group pulls both `orbital[sklearn]` and `orbital[pytorch]`.
- Version bumped to 0.7.0: a bare `pip install orbital` no longer ships scikit-learn. Getting-started docs now install `orbital[sklearn]` and state that the bare install is the shared core only.

**Code**
- `orbital._sklearn` and `orbital._pytorch` (private) each import their framework at module top and hold the framework-specific parsing. `parse_pipeline`, `parse_pytorch_model` and `types.guess_datatypes` keep their public docstrings and lazily import the module, translating a missing framework into `ImportError: ... Install it with: pip install orbital[sklearn|pytorch]` with the original cause chained. No framework-availability conditionals exist anywhere else.
- `ColumnType` carries `_onnx_elem_type` (ONNX `TensorProto` element type) instead of returning skl2onnx types, so the shared concat/inject logic in `orbital.ast` is skl2onnx-free. The skl2onnx mapping table lives in `_sklearn`.
- `EnsureConcatenatedInputs.concatenate_inputs()` became `uniform_type()`; the mixed-type error now names `ColumnType` classes (e.g. `DoubleColumnType`) rather than skl2onnx names.

**CI / tests**
- New `optional-frameworks` matrix job runs the suite with `uv sync --no-dev --extra test` plus `""` / `--extra sklearn` / `--extra pytorch`, using `uv run --no-sync` (a plain `uv run` would re-sync the dev group). The full-matrix `tests` job and `coverage` are unchanged.
- sklearn-dependent test modules `importorskip("sklearn")`; conftest imports sklearn datasets inside the fixtures. `tests/test_optional_frameworks.py` asserts the `[sklearn]` ImportError through the public API and runs only where scikit-learn is genuinely absent (the core and pytorch CI cells).

## Verification

- Dev environment: 371 passed / 31 skipped (Postgres unavailable locally); ruff, ruff format, mypy clean.
- Simulated install shapes: core 261 passed / 17 skipped, sklearn-only 367 / 34, pytorch-only 264 / 12. `import orbital` in the core shape loads no sklearn/skl2onnx/torch modules; `uv export --extra pytorch` resolves torch without scikit-learn/skl2onnx.
- A pipeline dumped with 0.6.0-era `ParsedPipeline.dump` loads and exports identical SQL in the core-only shape (`ColumnType` pickles carry only `is_passthrough`).

## Notes

- The `except ImportError` wrapper around `from . import _sklearn` also catches ImportErrors raised inside skl2onnx itself (e.g. a version incompatibility) and reports the extra hint; the real cause remains chained. Same trade-off as the pre-existing torch path.
- `guess_datatypes` remains skl2onnx-backed and therefore needs the `sklearn` extra. Making it framework-neutral (pandas dtypes → `ColumnType`) would be a separate change.


---

**Update:** `orbital.types.guess_datatypes` is also made framework-neutral in this PR. It maps a DataFrame's own dtypes to `ColumnType` directly (`onnx.helper.np_dtype_to_tensor_dtype`), no longer through skl2onnx's guesser — the mapping was never sklearn-specific, only implemented by borrowing skl2onnx. It now works in every install shape, including a bare `pip install orbital`. Results are unchanged for all previously-supported dtypes (verified against the old skl2onnx-based guesser). Whether a given model then requires uniform column types remains a concern of the caller's data and model, not of `guess_datatypes`.

title: Skip ibis dereferencing when preserving expressions
description:
Translation got much slower in #128 because `preserve()` appends to the table with one `mutate` per preserved group, 225 of them for `pipeline_boosted_tree_binary_classifier`. The variables a translator consumes hold columns of the table as it was when they were produced, so the expressions handed to `mutate` read an older projection than the table being extended. Ibis sees that and dereferences them: `bind` builds a `DerefMap` and `_fill_substitution_mappings` walks every column the table already has, hashing each stored expression. The table grows with every preserve, so each projection re-hashes everything that came before it.

I reproduced the regression first, on the same example the issue uses. These are the minimum of 3 runs with the model refit for each, so treat them as approximate; they line up with the table in the issue.

| phase | #127 (5e33b43) | #128 (4964303) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| generated SQL | 203,491 B | 184,317 B |
| `export_sql` | 4.87s | 26.30s |
| `orbital.translate` | 1.37s | 17.74s |
| ibis compile | 2.20s | 7.47s |
| raw DuckDB execution | 1.04s | 0.35s |

cProfile on `orbital.translate` after #128 puts 45.8s of its 50.3s in `preserve` -> `mutate` -> `bind` -> `dereference` -> `_fill_substitution_mappings`: 764 substitution maps over 370,951 field visits. That's the regression, the rest of the phase is unchanged.

Columns are only ever appended, so a reference to a column of an earlier table is the same value as the column of the current table under the same name. `Translator.preserve` now rebinds the expressions to the current table before mutating, which is enough for ibis to skip the dereference. The projection still carries every column forward and the generated SQL is byte-identical, so nothing from #128 is given back.

Before and after in one process on the same fitted model, `pipeline_boosted_tree_binary_classifier` (translation is the median of 4 alternating runs):

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `orbital.translate` | 19.6s | 1.80s |
| `export_sql` | 28.5s | 11.0s |
| raw DuckDB execution | 0.341s | 0.363s |
| generated SQL | 184,127 B | 184,127 B, same md5 |

The same comparison over all 15 examples in `examples/` gives byte-identical SQL for every one and execution unchanged within noise. Translation drops from 21.4s to 1.9s for the boosted tree binary classifier, 22.9s to 3.4s for the boosted tree classifier and 22.2s to 1.3s for the boosted tree regressor. The examples that barely preserve anything (elasticnet, lasso, lineareg) are unchanged.

The benchmarks now report the two phases separately. `test_translate` times `orbital.translate` on the example's input table, and `test_execute` exports the SQL first and times `con.raw_sql(sql).fetchall()`, so translation and compilation stay out of the execution number. The existing whole-example benchmark is still there, so the Perfall series keeps its history. Loaded examples are cached now, which keeps the suite at one model fit per example instead of one per benchmark.

Validation, all with a plain venv and `PYTHONPATH` rather than `uv sync`:

- `pytest` with the repo's addopts: 372 passed, 29 skipped (no postgres here), 95% coverage.
- `pytest benchmarks/ --benchmark-only --benchmark-time-unit=s --no-cov`: 45 passed.
- `examples/test_examples.sh` with `BACKEND=duckdb` and `BACKEND=sqlite`: all examples pass, the boosted tree classifier still skips itself on sqlite.
- `ruff check .`, `ruff format --check .` and `mypy`: clean.

I couldn't run `pre-commit run -a` in this environment: it builds its hook environments and the pip wheel cache is on another device, so the install fails with `[Errno 18] Invalid cross-device link`. I ran the three hooks it configures (`ruff`, `ruff-format`, `mypy`) directly instead.

The `coverage` job is red here, but only at the step that posts the coverage comment: fork pull requests get a read-only token, so it fails with `Resource not accessible by integration`. The summary step passes at 95%.

Closes #133

title: Return string class labels as strings instead of binary values
description:
A `LogisticRegression` trained on string class labels exports SQL that returns `output_label` as binary data instead of the class name:

```python
y = np.array(["setosa", "versicolor", "virginica"])[iris.target]
pipeline = Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("classifier", LogisticRegression())]).fit(X, y)
sql = orbital.export_sql("data", orbital.parse_pipeline(pipeline, features=features), dialect="duckdb")
# ... CASE WHEN ... = 0 THEN CAST('\x73\x65\x74\x6f\x73\x61' AS BLOB) ... END AS "output_label"
```

DuckDB returns the label as a list of bytes, SQLite (`UNHEX(...)`) and Postgres (`BYTEA`) as binary values, so it never equals `pipeline.predict(X)`. The probabilities are right, and tree models already return strings.

The class names reach `ArrayFeatureExtractor` through a STRING tensor initializer, and `get_initializer_data()` returned its `string_data` as bytes, which ibis turns into binary literals. String attributes are already decoded to `str` in `get_attr_value()`, so string initializers are now decoded the same way.

Added `test_logistic_regression_string_labels` to `tests/test_pipeline_e2e.py` (binary and multiclass, for each database fixture), which checks `output_label` against `pipeline.predict()`. The DuckDB and SQLite cases fail on main and pass here (Postgres is skipped locally). The full test suite passes (366 passed, 29 skipped for Postgres; `test_pytorch.py` not run), and ruff, ruff format and mypy are clean.

title: Skip PCA step tests when irlba 2.4.1 is broken on R < 4.4
description:
The oldrel-3 and oldrel-4 CI jobs fail on the `step_pca_sparse` and `step_pca_truncated` tests because irlba 2.4.1 (released 2026-10-05) is broken on R < 4.4. Its `oknum()` runs `is.atomic(scale)` on the default `scale = NULL`, which is `TRUE` before R 4.4.0, so every `irlba()` call errors with "LENGTH or similar applied to NULL object". I couldn't reproduce this locally (R 4.6.1, irlba 2.3.7), so the diagnosis comes from reading the irlba 2.4.1 source and the CI logs. The skip should turn the two failing jobs green, which this PR's own CI will confirm.

## Summary

- Adds `orbital.keras.src.models.functional.Functional()` for bare keras3 functional models with two or more outputs (e.g. `keras_model(inputs = inp, outputs = list(price = price, category = category))`), completing issue #185 alongside the torch trunk/heads support from #188.

- Fixes a bug in `set_pred_names()`: it previously assumed a regression result was always a single unnamed element and renamed positionally, which silently failed to rename a multi-output regression head's `.pred` entry when that head has its own hidden layer(s) before the final output. Now it renames the element actually named `.pred`, which also covers the original single-output case.

title: Add multi-output torch trunk/heads support (#185)
description:
## Summary
- Milestone 5a (torch half) of #185: adds `orbital.list()` for a network given as an explicit `list(trunk = ..., heads = list(...))`, each a bare `torch::nn_sequential()`, per the design doc's decision to require this shape rather than tracing an arbitrary `nn_module`'s `forward()` (out of scope; would need `torch::jit_trace()`).
- Reuses the existing single-chain walker/generator (`nn_sequential_layers()`, `nn_layer_exprs()`, `nn_output_eqs()`) unchanged: the trunk is walked once with every layer activated, then each head is walked once starting from the trunk's output columns, namespacing every generated column name by trunk/head so they can never collide.

An explicit, early error fires for names that don't match any head.
- Predictions are named `<prefix>_<head>*` (e.g. `.pred_price`, `.pred_category_class`, `.pred_category_<level>`) so two heads' output columns can never collide.
- `output_layer` is not supported yet for multi-output networks (explicit error) — out of scope for this PR.

title: Add BatchNorm/LayerNorm support to neural network extraction
description:
Closes #184 (Milestone 4 of the neural network support work, following #149/#177-#182).

## Summary

Extends the shared torch/keras3 walkers so a `Linear`/`Dense` layer can be followed by a BatchNorm or LayerNorm layer before its activation, covering every existing neural network entry point: bare `torch::nn_sequential()`, `mlp(engine = "brulee")`, bare keras3 `Sequential`, and `mlp(engine = "keras3")`.

- **BatchNorm** (`torch::nn_batch_norm1d()`, keras3's `layer_batch_normalization()`): a fixed per-channel affine transform read directly off the fitted layer's own stored running/moving statistics and learned scale/shift, folded into each neuron's own expression before its activation. `track_running_stats = FALSE` (torch) is rejected, since without stored running statistics the eval-time output depends on each prediction batch's own statistics, which orbital has no batch to compute over.
- **LayerNorm** (`torch::nn_layer_norm()`, keras3's `layer_layer_normalization()` -- not the R package's `layer_normalization()`, which maps to an unrelated preprocessing `Normalization` layer): normalizes each row over the layer's own neurons at inference time, so unlike BatchNorm this can't fold into one neuron's own independent expression. It materializes the layer's raw pre-norm values as their own intermediate columns first, then a shared mean/variance pair, then the final normalized value per neuron -- all correctly excluded from `output_layer`'s requested columns.
- For keras3, also adds support for a standalone `Activation` layer, since the standard idiom for combining `Dense` with BatchNorm/LayerNorm keeps the activation out of `Dense` itself (`layer_dense() |> layer_batch_normalization() |> layer_activation("relu")`).
- `estimate_orbital_size()`'s calibration is extended to account for both layer types' overhead, verified against real fitted networks.

Both correctness and calibration were verified numerically against real fitted torch and keras3 models (matching within float32/float64 tolerance, and within ~5% for the size estimate) before writing the test suite.
